subject: food-technology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on Food Safety, then mark my answer against the Edexcel spec.
promptWeak: Explain Food Safety for GCSE Edexcel Food Preparation & Nutrition simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Which micro-organism is used usefully to make bread and beer through fermentation?
questions.explain: Yeast is a useful micro-organism used in bread-making and brewing; it ferments sugars to produce carbon dioxide and alcohol. Not all micro-organisms are harmful.

questions.q: The fuzzy grey-green growth that appears on old bread is an example of:
questions.explain: Mould is a micro-organism that grows on food such as bread and cheese, producing visible spores. Some moulds produce toxins, so mouldy food should not be eaten.

questions.q: Which four conditions do bacteria need to multiply rapidly?
options: Heat above 100 degrees C, salt, acid and time
questions.explain: Bacteria multiply when they have warmth, moisture, food (nutrients) and time. Removing any one of these slows growth, which is the basis of safe storage.

questions.q: Under ideal warm conditions, roughly how often can bacteria double in number?
questions.explain: In the danger zone, one bacterium can divide about every 20 minutes, so numbers rise extremely quickly, which is why food must not be left warm for long.

questions.q: What is the temperature danger zone in which bacteria multiply most rapidly?
questions.explain: The danger zone is between 5 and 63 degrees C, where bacteria multiply fastest. Food should be kept below 5 degrees C or hot-held above 63 degrees C.

questions.q: A cooked curry is left on the worktop at 20 degrees C for four hours before being served. Why is this unsafe?
options: The curry loses all its vitamin C
The temperature is too cold for bacteria
It sat in the danger zone, allowing bacteria to multiply
questions.explain: 20 degrees C is within the danger zone, so over four hours bacteria multiply to unsafe levels. Cooked food should be cooled quickly and refrigerated within about 90 minutes.

questions.q: Which of these is a high-risk food that must be kept refrigerated?
questions.explain: High-risk foods are moist, high in protein and ready to eat, such as cooked meat, fish, dairy, eggs and cooked rice. They support rapid bacterial growth and need chilling.

questions.q: Why is cooked rice considered a high-risk food?
options: Bacillus cereus spores can survive cooking and multiply if it is left warm
It cannot be reheated at all
questions.explain: Bacillus cereus spores can survive cooking; if rice is left warm they germinate and produce toxins. Rice should be cooled quickly, chilled, and reheated only once until piping hot.

questions.q: What is cross-contamination?
options: Cooking food at too high a temperature
The transfer of harmful bacteria from one food or surface to another
Adding too much salt to food
questions.explain: Cross-contamination is the transfer of bacteria, usually from raw food to ready-to-eat food, via hands, chopping boards, knives or cloths.

questions.q: Which practice best prevents cross-contamination between raw and cooked foods?
options: Storing raw meat on the top shelf above cooked food
Wiping surfaces with a dirty cloth
Using the same board for raw chicken and salad
questions.explain: Colour-coded boards (e.g. red for raw meat, green for salad) keep raw and ready-to-eat foods separate. Raw meat should also be stored on the bottom shelf so it cannot drip onto other food.

questions.q: What is the correct temperature range for a domestic refrigerator?
questions.explain: A fridge should run between 0 and 5 degrees C to keep high-risk foods out of the danger zone and slow bacterial growth.

questions.q: At what temperature should a freezer be kept?
questions.explain: A freezer should be at -18 degrees C or below. Freezing does not kill bacteria but makes them dormant, so food stays safe while frozen.

questions.q: Which statement about freezing food is correct?
options: Once thawed, food should not be refrozen while raw
Frozen food never needs a use-by date
Freezing kills all bacteria in the food
You can safely refreeze thawed raw meat as often as you like
questions.explain: Freezing makes bacteria dormant, not dead. Thawed raw food should not be refrozen (unless cooked first), because bacteria can multiply during thawing.

questions.q: To be safe, food should be cooked or reheated until the core temperature reaches at least:
questions.explain: Food should reach a core temperature of at least 75 degrees C (held briefly) to destroy harmful bacteria. Food should be reheated only once.

questions.q: Hot food kept on display for service (hot-holding) must be kept at a temperature of at least:
questions.explain: Hot-held food must stay at 63 degrees C or above to keep it out of the danger zone and prevent bacteria multiplying while it waits to be served.

questions.q: Which bacterium is most commonly linked to undercooked poultry and raw eggs?
questions.explain: Salmonella is commonly associated with raw or undercooked poultry and eggs. Thorough cooking to 75 degrees C at the core destroys it.

questions.q: Campylobacter is the most common cause of food poisoning in the UK. It is mainly associated with:
questions.explain: Campylobacter is found mainly on raw poultry and is the most common cause of UK food poisoning; it is destroyed by thorough cooking and prevented by avoiding cross-contamination.

questions.q: Which is the single most important personal hygiene rule when preparing food?
questions.explain: Washing hands with warm water and soap, especially after handling raw meat or using the toilet, is the most important step in preventing the spread of bacteria.

questions.q: A food handler has a cut on their hand. What should they do before continuing to prepare food?
options: Cover it with a blue waterproof plaster
Rinse it with plain water only and carry on
questions.explain: Cuts should be covered with a brightly coloured (blue) waterproof plaster so they are easy to spot if they fall off, and to stop bacteria from the wound reaching the food.

questions.q: What does the 'use-by' date on a high-risk food such as fresh chicken mean?
options: The food is at its best quality but is still safe after this date
The date the food was made
The food should not be eaten after this date for safety reasons
The food can be eaten for a week afterwards
questions.explain: 'Use-by' is a safety date on perishable foods; the food should not be eaten or sold after it. 'Best before' is about quality, not safety.
